title: Financial and Operational Indicators Associated with Hospital Closure: Role of Hospital Type
content: Objective: To examine financial and operational indicators associated with subsequent hospital exit across US hospital types and propose a framework for future monitoring research. Methods: Medicare hospital cost-report files for 2011–2023 provided 36 533 analytic hospital-years from 4800 short-term acute care and critical access hospitals. Modeled years were 2011–2018, with filing assessed through 2021. Exit was defined by cessation of filing within the following three years; 816 positive hospital-years represented 334 distinct hospitals. Thirteen nationally standardized markers were analyzed separately within fourteen overlapping groups using logistic regression adjusted for log beds and year, with hospital-clustered standard errors. Results: Positive outcome proportions ranged from 0.9% in rural critical access hospitals to 6.5% in rural for-profit hospitals. Higher days cash on hand was associated with lower odds of exit in rural critical access hospitals (OR 0.10, 95% CI 0.04–0.31); the estimate for large urban hospitals was 0.71 (0.32–1.60). Occupancy estimates were 0.12 (0.06–0.26) in small rural prospective payment hospitals and 0.72 (0.46–1.12) in rural critical access hospitals. The leverage estimate was largest in large urban hospitals (2.40, 1.68–3.43). Conclusions: Estimated associations varied across hospital categories and warrant interpretation within their financing and organizational contexts. Differences between coefficients were not formally tested, and predictive performance was not assessed. External outcome validation and prospective model comparisons are needed before implementation.
